 Summer Hunger Rose 4 Points Among Low-Income Families With Children Despite Summer EBT
 Published Nov 07, 2026 7:45 PM EST 
 By
 Dorothy Brooks 
 RISTINA QUICLER | AFP via Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Low-income households with school-age children were 4 percentage points more likely to report not having enough to eat during the summer than during the rest of the year, according to a study published Nov. 5 in JAMA Network Open . In the first year of the federal Summer EBT program, known as SUN Bucks, states that delivered the benefit did not see a measurable drop in that hardship.
 The finding does not show that Summer EBT fails to help. Only about 30% of eligible households in participating states said they received the benefit, and the payment was small, which the researchers said may explain why no effect showed up.
 For families that depend on free or reduced-price school meals, summer break can mean covering up to 10 extra meals a week on the same budget. The study puts a number on that strain and raises questions about whether the new benefit is reaching the households that need it.
 The Summer Gap in Numbers
 Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and Children's Hospital of Philadelphia analyzed responses from 31,059 eligible households in the Census Bureau's Household Pulse Survey from January to September 2024. Eligible households had a child ages 5 to 17 and either received SNAP or had incomes at or below 185% of the federal poverty level.
 Among those households, food insufficiency, meaning sometimes or often not having enough to eat, rose by 4.0 percentage points in summer compared with other months. Households earning between 185% and 250% of the poverty level showed no significant change. Higher-income households saw a small rise of 0.7 points.
 Nationally, monthly food insufficiency ranged from 10.4% to 12.5% of households in 2024. The study's measure is narrower than the broader idea of food insecurity tracked by the USDA's Economic Research Service , which also counts families who cut the quality or variety of their meals.
 The pattern matches a long-standing concern among pediatricians and school officials. During the school year, many low-income children eat breakfast and lunch at school for free or at reduced cost, and that support disappears when school lets out.
 SUN Bucks Through Its First Year
 Summer EBT gives families $120 per eligible child for groceries , about $30 a month across the summer. Households that receive SNAP are enrolled automatically in participating states, while some others must apply. States choose each year whether to take part.
 In 2024, 37 states and Washington, D.C., participated, while 13 states did not. The researchers compared 33 states, including D.C., that distributed benefits between May 28 and Aug. 19, 2024, with 18 states that did not participate or paid benefits later. This approach, called a difference-in-differences analysis, looks at whether hardship changed more in states that paid benefits than in states that did not over the same months.
 The program was not significantly linked to a change in household food insufficiency, with an estimate of 0.8 percentage points and a wide range of uncertainty. The estimate for children's food insufficiency was also not significant, though the authors cautioned that differences in trends before the program make that result harder to interpret.
 Participation was low. Only 30.3% of eligible households in participating states reported receiving SUN Bucks, rising to 38.3% in the final survey period. Benefits arrived as a single lump sum, and the timing of those payments may have weakened their effect.
 The authors said the one-time payment "may have been too small to measurably impact food insufficiency," and that low participation and timing likely limited its reach.
 A Thin Survey and a Young Program
 The Household Pulse Survey had response rates of only 4.7% to 6.8%, with lower response among lower-income people. It also surveyed different households each time, so researchers could not track the same families over the summer.
 Food insufficiency was measured with a single question rather than the USDA's longer, 18-item food security scale, which may miss smaller changes. Some states and survey periods had small samples. The researchers also could not fully rule out other policies that changed at the same time.
 The first author was supported by the National Clinician Scholars Program, and the senior author by a federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality grant. The study evaluated only the first summer, and results in later years may differ as states improve enrollment and timing, so the finding should not be read as a verdict on the program.
 Finding Summer Food Help for Children
 Hunger during summer can affect children's health and readiness to learn when school resumes. Children in families just above SNAP income limits, households with irregular work hours, and families in states that skip the program may face the toughest gaps.
 Families can check whether their state offers SUN Bucks through the USDA's SUN Bucks page , which lists participating states, Tribes, and territories. Children in households receiving SNAP and certain other benefits are generally enrolled automatically in participating states, so parents should keep their mailing address current with their benefits office.
 Families who are not automatically enrolled may need to apply, often through their state's education or human services agency. The USDA's SUN Meals program offers free summer meals for children 18 and under at schools, parks, libraries, and other neighborhood sites, including in states that do not offer SUN Bucks. Families can find nearby locations with the USDA Summer Meals Site Finder .
 Local food banks, WIC for younger children and pregnant parents, and SNAP itself remain the main year-round supports. A pediatrician or school social worker can also connect families to local resources, and many clinics now screen for food insecurity at checkups.
 The next round of state participation decisions and the second year of data will show whether higher enrollment changes the picture. MedicalDaily will report on new evaluations as they are published.

 Key Questions Answered
 What did the study find? Food insufficiency rose 4 percentage points in summer among low-income households with school-age children.
 Did Summer EBT reduce summer hunger? In its first year, it was not linked to a measurable change, but low participation and a small benefit may explain that.
 How much is Summer EBT? $120 per eligible child for the summer, about $30 a month.
 How many eligible families got the benefit? About 30% of eligible households in participating states reported receiving it.
 Does this mean the program does not work? No. The study covered only the first year and used a survey with low response rates.
 Where can families find summer food help? Check the USDA SUN Bucks page, find SUN Meals sites, and contact local food banks or SNAP offices.
